title: Son of Adam (Luke 3:23–38)
hook: Luke's family tree goes back to Adam, son of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chiton he said to share: John told the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers to be fair right where they were. Your line was two coats, give one. Did the coat leave the house? Day four hundred fifty.

Lists of names in the Bible are easy to skim. But look where Luke puts his. Jesus has just been baptized in the Jordan. The heavens open, the Holy Ghost comes down in bodily shape like a dove, and a voice from heaven says: thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased. And right there, before Jesus says a word in public, Luke stops the story for a family tree. It's not filler. Where he puts it matters, and where it ends matters more.
screen: `EASY TO SKIM.` → `THOU ART MY BELOVED SON.` → `THEN, A FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: It starts, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus himself was beginning about the age of thirty years; being (as it was supposed) the son of Joseph." As it was supposed. Luke has already told us about the angel and Mary, and he doesn't let us forget it, even here. Then the list runs backward, father by father. Heli, Matthat, and on through a long run of names, to David, to Jesse, to Judah, to Isaac, to Abraham. And then it keeps going, past Abraham, past Noah, to Seth, and to the last line: "Who was of Henos, who was of Seth, who was of Adam, who was of God." Matthew's Gospel has a family tree too, but it runs forward and starts with Abraham, the father of Israel. Luke's runs backward, all the way past Abraham, to Adam. And adam, in Hebrew, is also the ordinary word for a human being; Genesis sets it beside adamah, the ground he was formed from. So a list carries something large. Christians read it as saying that this beloved Son belongs not only to one people, but to the whole human family. Here's an honest note. Between David and Joseph, Matthew and Luke give mostly different names. The Gospels never explain why. Christian writers have proposed answers: that one list traces Joseph's line and the other Mary's, or, from an early writer named Julius Africanus, that a custom of marrying a brother's widow gave Joseph both a natural and a legal father. The Church hasn't settled on one. What both trees agree on is the point Luke ends with: son of Adam, son of God.
screen: `AS IT WAS SUPPOSED, SON OF JOSEPH.` · `BACKWARD, PAST ABRAHAM, TO ADAM.` · `ADAM: HUMAN, FROM THE GROUND.` · `TWO TREES, DIFFERENT NAMES.` · then, large: `WHO WAS OF ADAM, WHO WAS OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: widen the circle. Settle, and breathe. Start with the people closest to you: your family, whoever that is for you. Hold them for a breath. Then widen: your street, your town, the people you passed today without noticing. Then wider: strangers in cities you'll never visit, people who speak languages you don't know, people you disagree with, people you find hard to love. Luke's list runs back to one father, Adam, for all of them. If you pray, you can pray for all of them together, the whole human family. If you don't, just let the circle stay that wide for a minute. The bell holds the time.
adam. Hebrew for a human being: the name Luke's family tree for Jesus runs back to, past Abraham, tying him to the whole human family. Today's word.
Your line: everyone's family. Today, look at one stranger and remind yourself, quietly: we're related. Day four hundred fifty.

howItsDone: At every Mass the Universal Prayer, or prayers of the faithful, asks God's help for the Church, the world, and all people in need, the whole human family.

original.note: Hebrew: Adam, a human being, related to adamah, the ground he was formed from.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of names to skip.
what it means: placed right after God calls Jesus his beloved Son, the list runs back to Adam, son of God, binding Jesus to all humanity.
what a scholar hears: it differs from Matthew's between David and Joseph; one early explanation is Julius Africanus's letter to Aristides, preserved by Eusebius.
